analysis.one_liner: Gives everyone a free yearly credit report and identity-theft protections, but permanently stops states from passing stronger credit-reporting laws.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 392-30, the Senate 95-2, and President Bush signed it into law on December 4, 2003, creating the right to a free annual credit report while permanently blocking states from enacting stricter credit-reporting protections.
analysis.plain_summary: This law (known as FACTA) amends the federal Fair Credit Reporting Act. It gives every consumer the right to one free credit report per year from each nationwide credit bureau, creates fraud alerts and identity-theft remedies, requires card receipts to print only the last five digits of a card number, and gives special alerts to service members deployed away from home. In exchange, it permanently extends federal preemption, meaning no state may pass a law after January 1, 2004 that gives consumers more protection than federal law on credit reporting. Consumers gained concrete new tools, but the states, which had been the main source of stronger credit rules, lost the power to go further, indefinitely.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers gain free annual credit reports from each nationwide bureau, one-call 90-day fraud alerts, seven-year extended alerts for identity-theft victims with free copies of their files, mandatory blocking of identity-theft information, card-number truncation on receipts, credit-score disclosures for mortgage applicants, and a permanent opt-out from affiliate marketing solicitations. Active-duty service members get dedicated alerts. Credit bureaus, banks, and lenders also gain: a single, permanent national standard that no state can tighten.

how_it_helps.text: Nationwide consumer reporting agencies must furnish a free credit report once every 12 months on request through a centralized source, and specialty agencies (medical, tenant, check-writing, insurance-claims files) must provide streamlined free access with a toll-free number.

Consumers can place a 90-day fraud alert with one call, referred to all bureaus; identity-theft victims who file a police report get a seven-year alert, exclusion from prescreened credit and insurance marketing for five years, and mandatory blocking of fraudulent information within four business days.
Active-duty military consumers can place an active-duty alert lasting at least 12 months, excluding them from prescreened offers for two years.
Businesses must print no more than the last five digits of credit or debit card numbers on receipts, and must provide transaction records to identity-theft victims and law enforcement at no charge.
Mortgage lenders must disclose the credit scores used in home loan decisions, and consumers may permanently opt out of affiliate sharing for marketing.

analysis.who_pays: Credit bureaus and lenders bear the cost of providing free reports, fraud alerts, dispute reinvestigations, and compliance procedures. Consumers pay a longer-term cost: because federal law is permanently supreme, no state can again require stronger accuracy rules, security freezes by statute, or tighter credit-score rules, and the risk-based pricing notice provision strips consumers of any private right of action, leaving enforcement solely to federal agencies.
analysis.who_pays_short: Credit bureaus and lenders; state-level consumer protections

drawbacks.text: Title VII repeals the scheduled expiration of federal preemption, permanently barring states from enacting credit-reporting protections stronger than federal law after January 1, 2004, which takes away the main avenue by which consumers had previously won tighter rules.
The risk-based pricing notice requirement denies consumers any civil action for noncompliance and rests enforcement exclusively with federal agencies.
Free annual reports must be requested only through a single centralized source, and consumers may not request a report directly from an individual bureau under that provision.

The opt-out from prescreened credit and insurance offers runs five years rather than permanently, and identity-theft blocking can be declined or rescinded if the agency determines the consumer obtained goods, services, or money from the transaction.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer benefits are real and widely used: free annual reports became one of the most exercised consumer rights in finance, and the fraud-alert and blocking tools are the foundation of today's identity-theft response. But the bill was a package deal. The price consumers paid was permanent: the strongest engine of credit-reporting protection had been state legislatures like California's, and this law forecloses that route forever. An honest supporter would say the free-report and identity-theft gains outweigh that loss; an honest critic would say the industry accepted modest new duties precisely in order to buy a permanent ceiling on stricter state rules.

outcome.mechanism: It sailed through both chambers with almost no opposition, went to a conference committee, and President Bush signed it as Public Law 108-159 on December 4, 2003.

narrative.text: Introduced June 26, 2003, the bill cleared the House Financial Services Committee 63-3, was reported September 4, and passed the House 392-30 on September 10, 2003.

The House considered it under a rule allowing amendments; members including Reps. Waters, Lee, Sanders, Frank, and Kanjorski offered amendments during floor debate, and the bill passed with permanent preemption intact.
The Senate struck the House text and substituted the language of S. 1753, then passed it 95-2 on November 5, 2003; only 2 of 48 Democrats and no Republicans voted no.
A conference report filed November 21, 2003 was agreed to 379-49 in the House and by unanimous consent in the Senate, and was signed into law December 4, 2003 as Public Law 108-159.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit bureaus and financial institutions came out ahead: they gained a permanent national standard that blocks states from ever again passing stricter credit-reporting laws, in exchange for free annual reports and identity-theft procedures. Consumers did gain real, lasting tools, especially free credit reports and fraud alerts, but the ceiling on state-level protection is locked in permanently.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Credit bureaus and lenders; consumers got real tools too

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelming in both parties: in the House, 221 of 228 Republicans and 171 of 205 Democrats voted yes on passage (final conference vote: 224-3 R, 155-45 D); in the Senate, 51 of 51 Republicans and 43 of 48 Democrats voted yes, with only 2 Democrats opposed.

industries.note: The law locks the bureaus into their role as the permanent, nationally regulated gatekeepers of consumer credit data, and frees them from ever-tightening state rules. In exchange they must give free annual reports, honor fraud alerts, and block identity-theft information, duties that created the consumer tools Americans still use.

industries.industry: Banks, credit card issuers, and other lenders
industries.note: Lenders gained a single permanent federal standard, ending the threat of stronger state credit-reporting and risk-based-pricing laws, while absorbing compliance duties like address-change verification and negative-information notices. Their core interest in this bill, a uniform national floor, ran against consumers' ability to win stronger rules in the states.

Title VI excludes communications about employee misconduct investigations from the consumer-disclosure rules, so employers can investigate workers without triggering disclosure requirements, though workers must still get a summary if the investigation leads to an adverse action.

The law bars selling, transferring, or placing for collection any debt that has been identified as resulting from identity theft, and requires collectors notified of fraud to pass that notice along and give victims full dispute rights.
